In particular, the regulation contemplates submitting periodic safety reports for medicines holding sanitary registration, allowing the regulatory authority to continuously assess their safety profile and adopt appropriate sanitary measures when necessary.

However, the cited regulation mainly refers to medicines authorized for marketing, and does not expressly establish the obligation to submit specific annual safety reports for products in the clinical research phase, nor does it define a set format for such reports.
q_5_2_fuente: Ley de Medicamentos (Gaceta Oficial N° 37.006 del 03 de agosto de 2000), Article 49. Normas de la Junta Revisora de Productos Farmacéuticos (5ta Revisión, Julio de 1998), Chapter III – Group H (Pharmacovigilance).
q_5_3_directa: Yes, the Comisión de Bioética y Bioseguridad (CoBioBios) of the MCT and FONACIT has the authority to request information on site during the research's conduct. In addition, institutional bioethics commissions must declare their willingness to follow up on bioethical aspects.
q_5_3_ampliada: The NRA (through CoBioBios, if the project is funded by MCT/FONACIT) may request on-site visits to verify compliance. For pharmaceutical products in general, sponsoring laboratories are committed to reporting to the INHRR any undescribed effect arising from the product's pharmacological activity, after its approval.
q_5_3_fuente: Código de Bioética y Bioseguridad (Part III, Section B, Item 8); Código de Bioética y Bioseguridad (Part III, Section D, Item 3); Normas de la Junta Revisora de Productos Farmacéuticos (5ta Revisión, Julio de 1998) (Chapter III, Group I, Item 6).
q_5_4_directa: Yes. Any modification to the authorized marketing conditions or substantial post-registration changes, including dosage or indications, must be approved in advance by the JRPF.
q_5_4_ampliada: The JRPF requires any modification to a product's previously authorized conditions (which would include significant changes to a clinical trial's approved protocol) to be approved in advance. Post-registration modifications requiring authorization include changes to indications and dosage, which must attach recently published clinical studies supporting the requested change.
q_5_4_fuente: Normas de la Junta Revisora de Productos Farmacéuticos (5ta Revisión, Julio de 1998) (Chapter III, Group I, Item 3); Normas de la Junta Revisora de Productos Farmacéuticos (5ta Revisión, Julio de 1998) (Chapter III, Group J, Item 9).
q_5_5_directa: Not specified in official regulations.
q_5_5_ampliada: The regulation focuses on ensuring compensation for harm or injury during the study, and a "Compassionate Use Medicine" category exists for patients with serious, disabling conditions who have no comparable therapeutic alternatives. However, the sponsor's specific obligation to guarantee participants access to the investigational treatment once the clinical trial ends is not addressed.
q_5_5_fuente: No specific regulation was identified on this point.
q_6_1_directa: No specific organic law on personal data protection exists in Venezuela. However, data protection is a constitutional right, and its violation is penalized under the Ley de Delitos Informáticos.
q_6_1_ampliada: Although Venezuela lacks a comprehensive data protection law similar to the European GDPR, a legal framework exists to protect clinical trial participants' personal information. The Constitution of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela establishes, in Article 28, the right of Habeas Data, guaranteeing everyone access to their data in public or private records and the right to request its rectification or deletion. Article 60 protects the right to privacy and confidentiality. The Ley de Delitos Informáticos, in Articles 20 and 22, also penalizes, with two to six years of imprisonment, anyone who, without consent, uses, modifies, or discloses personal information contained in computer systems. Investigators and sponsors therefore have a strict legal obligation to guarantee the confidentiality and proper handling of subjects' data.
q_6_1_fuente: Constitución de la República Bolivariana de Venezuela (Articles 28 and 60); Ley de Delitos Informáticos (Articles 20 and 22).
q_6_2_directa: No. Vaccines, classified as Biological Products, are subject to rigorous oversight and examination by the INHRR and, in the interest of public health, may require prior authorization for each manufacturing batch.
q_6_2_ampliada: The Ministry of Health, through the INHRR, is responsible for overseeing and examining biological products before they are marketed. For biological products, if necessary in the interest of public health, each finished product manufacturing batch will undergo prior authorization, and marketing will be conditional on its compliance, including authorization of source materials and intermediate products.
q_6_2_fuente: Ley de Medicamentos (Gaceta Oficial N° 37.006 del 03 de agosto de 2000) (Title IV, Chapter III, Articles 26 and 27); Normas de la Junta Revisora de Productos Farmacéuticos (5ta Revisión, Julio de 1998) (Chapter I, Group B, "Producto Biológico").
q_6_3_directa: Yes, the Ley sobre Transplante de Órganos y Materiales Anatómicos en Seres Humanos regulates the disposition of organs and tissues for research and teaching purposes. In addition, the Normas Venezolanas de Biodisponibilidad y Bioequivalencia detail the handling of biological samples for pharmacokinetic studies.
q_6_3_ampliada: The Ley sobre Transplante de Órganos governs the disposition of anatomical materials for research purposes, requiring that research only be conducted if the knowledge cannot be obtained by other methods, and that it be grounded in prior animal experimentation. In the pharmacokinetic area, the regulation requires defining the sample type (blood, serum, plasma, etc.), sampling times covering at least 80% of the area under the curve (AUC), and specifying the sample's treatment and storage.
q_6_3_fuente: Ley sobre Transplante de Órganos y Materiales Anatómicos en Seres Humanos (Chapter I, Article 1 and 2, Item 11); Normas Venezolanas de Biodisponibilidad y Bioequivalencia de Productos Farmacéuticos (Resolución No 212, Gaceta Oficial N° 38.499) (Article 5, Section a.5.1, a.7.2, and a.7.3).
q_6_4_directa: Yes, the Código de Bioética y Bioseguridad sets out specific ethical considerations for vulnerable populations' participation. In addition, the Norma de Medicamentos de Servicio regulates products in the clinical research or compassionate use phase, such as the Early Access Medicine and the Compassionate Use Medicine.
q_6_4_ampliada: The Código de Bioética y Bioseguridad details special conditions for groups such as minors (excluded if the research can be conducted in adults), sick or mentally disabled persons (only if they are the only ones available), pregnant women, and captive groups (detained or subordinate persons). The Norma de Medicamentos de Servicio includes the "Early Access Medicine," defined as a product in the clinical research phase proposed to extend or improve quality of life, constituting a superior option to what exists on the market, with no commercial purpose.
q_6_4_fuente: Código de Bioética y Bioseguridad (Chapter 1, Standards 10, 11, and 12); Norma de Medicamentos de Servicio (2015) (Chapter II, Section I, Article 9, Items 3 and 4).

q_1_1_directa: The main authority responsible is the Chemistry Food and Drugs Division (CFDD), which operates under the Ministry of Health, assisted by the Drug Advisory Committee.
q_1_1_ampliada: The CFDD is the point of contact for receiving and processing technical documentation, including clinical studies, submitted as part of a New Drug Submission (NDS). The Minister of Health formally makes the decision to approve or withdraw new drugs, based on the Drug Advisory Committee's advice.
q_1_1_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations (Second Schedule, Division 3, paragraph 7, Division 8, paragraph 3); Detailed Requirements For New Drug Submission (Instruction 1, Section 3); Guidelines for Agents - New Drug Registration and Supplemental Application Submission (Page 2).
q_1_2_directa: Health research related to medicines is governed primarily by the Food and Drugs Act (Chapter 30:01) and its Food and Drugs Regulations.
q_1_2_ampliada: These regulations define what constitutes a drug and establish the requirements for its sale, labeling, and maintenance of standards. They also create the legal structure for submitting new drug applications, which require submitting technical and clinical data.
q_1_2_fuente: Food and Drugs Act, Chapter 30:01 (Chapter 30:01 title, Section 2, 9); Food and Drugs Regulations (Regulation 1, Regulation 32); Detailed Requirements For New Drug Submission (Instruction 1).
q_1_3_directa: Research authorization is governed by the Food and Drugs Regulations, specifically under Division 3 of the Second Schedule, which sets out the rules for submitting and approving New Drugs, as well as the conditions for research aimed at data collection.
q_1_3_ampliada: A drug proposed for a new use, or a condition of use that has not previously been imported or used in the country, is considered a "new drug." The regulation explicitly permits importing and using these drugs to collect clinical and scientific data by qualified investigators, provided strict notification and written authority conditions are met. It should be noted that this framework does not constitute a "clinical trial authorization" in the modern sense, but rather a regulatory exemption allowing the use of an unregistered product for research purposes, under strict supervision and reporting conditions, in the context of collecting data for an eventual commercial registration application.
q_1_3_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations (Second Schedule, Division 3, paragraph 1, 10, 15); Detailed Requirements For New Drug Submission (Instruction 1, Section 3).
q_1_4_directa: This does not arise from the regulations reviewed.
q_1_4_ampliada: The main legal framework, focused on product regulation, does not include ethical review as part of the regulatory authority's (CFDD) process. However, conducting any research involving human subjects in the country is subject to international ethical standards (Declaration of Helsinki, ICH-GCP) and to health institutions' (hospitals and universities) internal policies. These institutions require the research protocol, informed consent form, and other relevant documents to be reviewed and approved by their own institutional Research Ethics Committee (REC) before allowing any study activity to begin on their premises.
q_1_4_fuente: No specific regulation was identified on this point.
q_1_5_directa: No legally prescribed sequence exists. REC approval and the application to the Regulatory Authority (NRA) are parallel, independent processes.
q_1_5_ampliada: The law does not stipulate a sequential order between ethical and regulatory approval. The NRA (CFDD) evaluates the new drug's dossier, while the REC evaluates the protocol's ethics and participant protection. In practice, sponsors typically manage both submissions in parallel to optimize timelines. It is advisable to have the protocol and informed consent in their final version before submitting them to both entities. The REC's approval letter is not an explicit requirement for the initial submission to the CFDD, but it is indispensable for beginning recruitment at the research site.
q_1_5_fuente: No specific regulation was identified on this point.
q_1_6_directa: No official national registry or government accreditation system exists for Research Ethics Committees (RECs) in Trinidad and Tobago.
q_1_6_ampliada: REC oversight takes place at the institutional level. No central body registers, accredits, or oversees them. However, several RECs in the country participate in the Caribbean Network of Research Ethics Committees (CANREC), an initiative of the Caribbean Public Health Agency (CARPHA) that seeks to promote cooperation and harmonize ethical review standards across the region. This participation in regional networks serves as a self-regulation and quality-improvement mechanism.
q_1_6_fuente: Caribbean Network of Research Ethics Committees (CANREC).
q_1_7_directa: No official government public national registry dedicated to Research Ethics Committees (RECs) exists in Trinidad and Tobago. Information on and oversight of these committees is handled mainly at the level of each health institution.
q_1_7_ampliada: Ethics committees' governance and formation fall directly on individual health institutions. For example, the North Central Regional Health Authority (NCRHA) operates its own independent committee. Currently, the State does not have a public database or government portal centralizing the national registry of these committees. However, at the regional level, CARPHA coordinates CANREC. This network gathers information from member states' RECs to build a mutual information-sharing base. Although CANREC works to provide a regional registry of approved research, this does not substitute for a freely accessible national public registry of committees.
q_1_7_fuente: Caribbean Network of Research Ethics Committees; NCRHA- Ethics Committee.
q_1_8_directa: Yes. Importing or manufacturing a "new drug" for research purposes must be reported to the Minister or the CFDD Director, and the research must have the Minister's written authorization before it can begin.
q_1_8_ampliada: A drug meeting the definition of "new drug" (by containing an untested substance, a new combination, or a new proposed use) requires the NRA to be informed of its identifying name/brand before import. Investigators must receive the Minister's written authority (advised by the Drug Advisory Committee) before proceeding to collect clinical data.
q_1_8_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations (Second Schedule, Division 3, paragraph 1, 10, Division 8, paragraph 16).
q_2_1_directa: The regulation does not specifically define the term "sponsor," instead directing obligations to the "manufacturer" or "importer" submitting the New Drug Submission (NDS) or research documentation.
q_2_1_ampliada: The "manufacturer" is defined as the person, firm, partnership, or corporation selling a drug to the public or to a wholesaler under its own name or trademark. These entities are responsible for submitting clinical study data to support the product's registration.
q_2_1_fuente: Food and Drugs Act, Chapter 30:01 (Section 2, definition of "manufacturer"); Food and Drugs Regulations (Second Schedule, Division 3, paragraph 2).
q_2_2_directa: Yes. The documentation must be submitted by the Importer, Manufacturer, or Agent, with a specified domicile and address in Trinidad and Tobago.
q_2_2_ampliada: Although the term "legal representative" is not used, the official forms (Form C and D) require the applicant, whether the Importer, Manufacturer, or Agent, to state their name and address in Trinidad and Tobago and to sign the application as such, ensuring local accountability.
q_2_2_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations (Third Schedule, Form C - New Drug Submission, field 1; Form D - Supplement to New Drug Submission).
q_2_3_directa: Yes. It must comply with submitting the complete technical documentation, ensure manufacturing takes place under adequate conditions (GMP), and take on pharmacovigilance obligations, including the immediate reporting of unexpected adverse events.
q_2_3_ampliada: For domestically manufactured drugs, the manufacturer must obtain a Certificate from the Director confirming the drug has been manufactured, preserved, stored, and tested under adequate conditions. For all new drugs, the manufacturer or importer must inform the Minister as soon as possible of any report of injury, toxicity, or sensitivity reaction associated with clinical uses.
q_2_3_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations (Second Schedule, Division 3, paragraph 9, Division 8, paragraph 2, 14).
q_2_4_directa: Not specified in official regulations.
q_2_4_ampliada: The regulation provided is directed mainly at the "Agent" submitting the application to the CFDD. It does not detail the role, definition, or specific requirements a Contract Research Organization (CRO) must meet when acting on the sponsor's behalf.
q_2_4_fuente: Guidelines for Agents - New Drug Registration and Supplemental Application Submission (Page 2); Food and Drugs Regulations.
q_2_5_directa: Yes. The drug must be imported or used by "qualified investigators" who have the necessary "facilities" for the research, and who have obtained the Minister's written authority to conduct that study.
q_2_5_ampliada: The importer or manufacturer must ensure that the person to whom the experimental drug is sold is a qualified investigator with adequate facilities, and must obtain written assurance that the drug will only be used under their direction. The Minister's written authority is issued following the Drug Advisory Committee's advice.
q_2_5_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations (Second Schedule, Division 3, paragraph 10, Division 8, paragraph 16).
q_2_6_directa: Yes. Sponsors or importers must ensure the Principal Investigator and their team are duly qualified, by training and experience, for the study. This fitness is actively assessed by both the national regulatory authority and institutional ethics committees.
q_2_6_ampliada: Trinidad and Tobago's regulations explicitly require experimental drugs to be supplied to and used only by qualified investigators. To validate this competence, the sponsor is responsible for selecting suitable personnel to conduct the study. This is formally demonstrated by submitting the principal and secondary investigators' updated curriculum vitae (CV) within "Part A" of the trial registration application form. In parallel, local ethics committees play a vital role in this verification. For example, the NCRHA's Ethics Committee has the regulatory objective of examining an investigator's credentials through their CV and requiring any supplementary documentation (such as GCP training), thereby ensuring subject protection.
q_2_6_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations, Second Schedule, Division 3, Paragraph 10; Clinical Trial Registration Form; NCRHA- Ethics Committee.
q_2_7_directa: Trinidad and Tobago's regulations do not establish explicit requirements for the sponsor to take out insurance or set up a compensation plan for trial participants in the event of research-related harm.
q_2_7_ampliada: No specific regulation was identified on this point.
q_2_7_fuente: No specific regulation was identified on this point.
q_3_1_directa: Yes. Submitting the New Drug Submission (NDS) is structured into four sections (dossiers) that must be submitted in duplicate: Administrative, Chemistry Documentation, Clinical (including non-clinical data and bioequivalence studies), and Other (Sections 4-7).
q_3_1_ampliada: The Clinical section must contain Pharmacodynamic data (general pharmacology, efficacy tests), Pharmacokinetic data (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, bioequivalence), Pharmacotherapeutic data (therapeutic uses, clinical trials, therapeutic equivalence), and Toxicity data of all types, whether published or in-house. The submission also requires the NDS forms (A, C, D) to be correctly completed.
q_3_1_fuente: Detailed Requirements For New Drug Submission (Instruction 1, 5; Sections 1, 2, 3, 4-7; Pharmaceutical Documentation).
q_3_2_directa: Yes. Submission must be made through a single Electronic Application (implemented via Google Forms) that unifies the former Forms A, B, C, and D.
q_3_2_ampliada: The documentary dossiers must be submitted in duplicate. The electronic platform allows 24/7 access and uploading of scanned documents, which requires the Agent to have a valid Google (Gmail) account for the application to be considered complete. An indispensable technical requirement for completing the application is that the Agent must use a valid Google (Gmail) account. The Google Forms platform requires this authentication to allow the dossier's scanned documents to be uploaded, and without it, the application cannot be completed and submitted.
q_3_2_fuente: Guidelines for Agents - New Drug Registration and Supplemental Application Submission (Page 2); Detailed Requirements For New Drug Submission (Instruction 5).
q_3_3_directa: Yes. The official maximum time frame for the Minister to notify the applicant of the decision on a New Drug Submission (NDS) or a supplement is one hundred and twenty (120) days from submission.
q_3_3_ampliada: This 120-day time frame applies to evaluating the complete NDS dossier, which includes administrative, quality (CMC), non-clinical, and clinical data. It is not a specific time frame for authorizing a clinical trial protocol in isolation. The evaluation determines whether the "new drug" as a whole is considered safe for the proposed use, including its use in the planned clinical research. This product-registration-integrated approach distinguishes Trinidad and Tobago's process from clinical trial authorization systems in other jurisdictions.
q_3_3_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations (Second Schedule, Division 3, paragraph 7, Division 8, paragraph 12).
q_3_4_directa: Yes, submitting a New Drug Submission requires advance payment of a non-refundable registration fee of TT$750.00, and supplements (variations) cost TT$100.00.
q_3_4_ampliada: The fee must be paid in advance, and the Comptroller of Accounts' receipt must be attached to the new drug application. This fee covers the administrative cost of processing the application, which includes reviewing the clinical and technical documentation.
q_3_4_fuente: Detailed Requirements For New Drug Submission (Instruction 6); Food and Drugs Regulations (Second Schedule, Division 3, paragraph 2, 5; Third Schedule, Form E).
q_3_5_directa: No. Trinidad and Tobago's local regulations do not mandatorily require registering a clinical trial in a public database before it begins.
q_3_5_ampliada: Although the law allows the Minister to maintain a registry of approved new drugs and requires approval notices to be published in the Gazette, no obligation is established for the sponsor or investigator to publicly register (e.g., on an international platform) the clinical trial protocol before it begins.
q_3_5_fuente: Food and Drugs Act, Chapter 30:01 (Section 25, subsection 1, item l); Food and Drugs Regulations.
q_3_6_directa: Yes, approval certificates or compliance notifications from other countries' regulatory authorities are recognized and accepted, provided the conditions set out in the regulation are met.
q_3_6_ampliada: For imported drugs, the applicant may submit documentation from Canada's Food and Drug Directorate, the US FDA, the UK's Ministry of Health, or Australia's Department of Health. Safety certificates from other official bodies are also accepted if the Minister considers them to have the appropriate expertise and facilities to guarantee the new drug's safety.
q_3_6_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations (Second Schedule, Division 3, paragraph 3, item f, i-v).
q_3_7_directa: The process begins with selecting the team and notifying the NRA, followed by ensuring the investigator's qualifications and facilities, and concludes with obtaining the Minister's written authority.
q_3_7_ampliada:
Planning and dossier preparation: The sponsor prepares the complete NDS dossier, including the clinical trial protocol, the Investigator's Brochure, and the draft informed consent.

Selecting the investigator and institution: The importer/manufacturer identifies a qualified investigator with adequate facilities in Trinidad and Tobago.

Ethics Committee submission and approval (Practical Step): The protocol, informed consent, and other relevant documents are submitted to the research site's institutional REC for review and approval. This step is carried out in parallel with preparation for the NRA.

NRA notification (Pre-import): The CFDD is informed of the new drug intended for research.

Submitting the NDS to the NRA: The local Agent submits the complete NDS application, including the clinical documentation, through the CFDD's electronic form, and pays the corresponding fee.

Investigator's written commitment: The sponsor obtains a written commitment from the investigator that the drug will be used exclusively under their direction.

NRA review (120-day time frame): The CFDD and the Drug Advisory Committee review the NDS dossier.

Obtaining Written Authority: If the review is satisfactory, the Minister of Health issues the written authority for the investigator to conduct the research.

IP labeling and import: The Investigational Product (IP) is labeled with the statement "To Be Used By Qualified Investigators Only," and it is then imported for the study to begin.
q_3_7_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations (Second Schedule, Division 3, paragraph 10, 12, Division 8, paragraph 16).
q_4_1_directa: Yes. The Investigational Product's (IP) inner label and outer label must bear the mandatory statement "To Be Used By Qualified Investigators Only."
q_4_1_ampliada: This statement must be present to clearly identify the product as restricted research material, ensuring its sale or use is limited exclusively to qualified investigators participating in the clinical study, and not to the general public.
q_4_1_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations (Second Schedule, Division 3, paragraph 10, item b, Division 8, paragraph 16, item b, ii).
q_4_2_directa: Yes. The registration process requires Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) certification, or proof that the drug was manufactured under adequate conditions.
q_4_2_ampliada: For imported drugs, the required Certificate of Pharmaceutical Product (CPP) must attest to the manufacturing laboratory's Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP). For locally manufactured drugs, the manufacturer may not sell the finished product without a Certificate issued by the Director certifying that manufacturing, preservation, storage, and testing were carried out under adequate conditions.
q_4_2_fuente: Detailed Requirements For New Drug Submission (Section 1.2); Food and Drugs Regulations (Second Schedule, Division 8, paragraph 2).
q_4_3_directa: Yes. Granting written authority for the investigator to use the new experimental drug includes permission to import or manufacture it for that specific purpose.
q_4_3_ampliada: The new drug may be imported or manufactured in specific quantities for use by qualified investigators for the purpose of collecting clinical data. The Minister may also grant written permission to import specific quantities to prepare or complete the New Drug Submission.
q_4_3_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations (Second Schedule, Division 3, paragraph 10, 12, Division 8, paragraph 16).
q_5_1_directa: Yes. The manufacturer or importer must inform the Minister "as soon as possible" of any report of unexpected side effects, injury, toxicity, or sensitivity reaction associated with the new drug's clinical uses, studies, or tests.
q_5_1_ampliada: The obligation falls on the manufacturer or importer, who must ensure timely reporting of any unexpected adverse event, injury, toxicity, or sensitivity related to the new drug's research, seeking to protect public health through prompt NRA action.
q_5_1_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations (Second Schedule, Division 3, paragraph 9, Division 8, paragraph 14).
q_5_2_directa: Not specified in official regulations.
q_5_2_ampliada: The regulatory framework focuses on immediately reporting unexpected or serious adverse events. No explicit provision in the regulation requires the sponsor or manufacturer to submit periodic safety reports, such as Development Safety Update Reports (DSURs), during the study's conduct.
q_5_2_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations (Second Schedule, Division 3, paragraph 9, Division 8, paragraph 14).
q_5_3_directa: Not specified in official regulations.
q_5_3_ampliada: The regulation details the documentation required for the initial new drug submission (NDS) and for reporting significant changes. However, the current regime does not establish an obligation to submit periodic progress or follow-up reports (e.g., quarterly or annual) on the trial to the NRA.
q_5_3_fuente: Food and Drugs Act, Chapter 30:01; Food and Drugs Regulations.
q_5_4_directa: Yes. Amendments constituting a "material change" to the information submitted in the original NDS require submitting a supplement (Form D) and obtaining the Minister's approval.
q_5_4_ampliada: A material change includes variations in the conditions of use (indications and route of administration), labeling, packaging, pharmaceutical form, dosage, or strength, purity, or quality. The sponsor must submit Form D together with technical documentation supporting that quality and safety are not affected by the change, and pay the TT$100 fee.
q_5_4_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations (Second Schedule, Division 3, paragraph 5, items a-f); Third Schedule, Form E.
q_5_5_directa: Not specified in official regulations.
q_5_5_ampliada: Current regulations cover the drug's registration, manufacturing, and safety obligations, but do not address the sponsor's responsibilities regarding continued supply of the experimental treatment to clinical trial participants once the study ends (post-trial access).
q_5_5_fuente: Food and Drugs Act, Chapter 30:01; Food and Drugs Regulations.
q_6_1_directa: Yes. The applicable law is the Data Protection Act, 2011 (Act No. 13 of 2011). This law has only been partially implemented.
q_6_1_ampliada: The Data Protection Act, 2011 establishes the legal framework for personal data protection in Trinidad and Tobago. The law defines "sensitive personal information" to include data on an individual's physical or mental health. Although only some parts of the law have formally entered into force, the "General Privacy Principles" it contains (such as the need for consent, purpose limitation, data security, and safeguards for international transfer) must be considered the compliance standard. For a clinical trial, this means the Informed Consent Form must explicitly detail what health data will be collected, how it will be used, protected, stored, and whether it will be transferred outside Trinidad and Tobago. The law stipulates that international transfers may only be made to jurisdictions with "comparable safeguards," an assessment that is the sponsor's responsibility.
q_6_1_fuente: Data Protection Act, 2011 (Act No. 13 of 2011).
q_6_2_directa: No specific regulations or guidelines are available for vaccine clinical trials, so they are governed by the general New Drug Submission (NDS) requirements.
q_6_2_ampliada: Vaccines meeting the definition of "new drug" must go through the standard NDS approval pathway, requiring the submission of clinical, toxicological, and manufacturing data. Approval notifications show that vaccines are evaluated under this same framework.
q_6_2_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations (Second Schedule, Division 3, paragraph 1); Approval of New Drugs Notification.
q_6_3_directa: Not specified in official regulations.
q_6_3_ampliada: The regulatory framework focuses on regulating pharmaceutical product samples (IP or active ingredient) required for quality control and registration. Trinidad and Tobago has no specific regulation for handling, collecting, or using human biological samples in clinical research.
q_6_3_fuente: Food and Drugs Act, Chapter 30:01; Food and Drugs Regulations.
q_6_4_directa: Yes, sections dedicated to regulating Alternative/Herbal Medicines exist, whose evaluation must include clinical, safety, and pharmacology aspects reviewed by the Drug Advisory Committee and a Herbal Sub-Committee.
q_6_4_ampliada: The review of herbal medicines contemplates 14 evaluation points covering the product's pharmacology, safety, and clinical aspects.
q_6_4_fuente: Detailed Requirements For New Drug Submission (Alternative/Herbal Medicines in Trinidad and Tobago section).

q_1_1_directa: The main authority responsible for health regulation is the Standards and Regulation Division (SRD) of the Ministry of Health and Wellness.
q_1_1_ampliada: The Standards and Regulation Division was created in March 1999 and has the mandate to improve the quality of health services and oversee the sector. Its structure includes the Pharmaceutical and Regulatory Affairs subsidiary. In addition, the Ethics and Medico-Legal Affairs Panel (EMLAP) is the specific advisory body handling the review of research protocols involving human subjects.
q_1_1_fuente: Standards and Regulation Division – Ministry of Health and Wellness of Jamaica (Chapter: Standards and Regulation Division, paragraphs 1 and 2); (Chapter: Advisory Panels, paragraph 2).
q_1_2_directa: Health research is governed primarily by the Food and Drugs Act, 1964 (and its 1975 Regulations) and the Ministry of Health and Wellness's Guidelines for the Conduct of Research on Human Subjects.
q_1_2_ampliada: The Food and Drugs Act, 1964, together with its 1975 Regulations, constitutes the fundamental legislative framework for regulating drugs and new drugs. The Ministry's Guidelines complement this framework, establishing the ethical principles, informed consent requirements, and detailed procedures for reviewing research protocols involving human subjects.
q_1_2_fuente: Food and Drugs Act, 1964 (Act 46 of 1964) (Chapter: Legislative framework, paragraph 1); (Section 1, paragraphs 1 and 2); Guidelines for the Conduct of Research on Human Subjects (Chapter: Introduction, paragraph 1).
q_1_3_directa: Clinical trial authorization is governed by the legal framework of the Food and Drugs Act, 1964, which empowers the Minister to make regulations, and the Food and Drugs Regulations, 1975, which specifically regulates licensing for "new drugs."
q_1_3_ampliada: The Food and Drugs Regulations, 1975 define what a "new drug" is and prohibit its import, sale, or manufacture without a license issued by the Minister. Specific conditions are also established for importing new drugs for research purposes. Protocols must be evaluated according to the Ministry of Health's guidelines.
q_1_3_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations, 1975 (LN 65/1975) (Regulation 64, paragraph 1); (Regulation 65, paragraph 1); Guidelines for the Conduct of Research on Human Subjects (Chapter: Research Protocol Review, paragraph 2).
q_1_4_directa: Yes, approval from an ethics committee is required at two levels: the local Institutional Ethics Panel for all protocols before they begin, and the Ministry of Health's Ethics and Medico-Legal Affairs Panel (EMLAP) for central oversight of research involving human subjects.
q_1_4_ampliada: The Ministry's Guidelines establish that research protocols must be reviewed and approved by the local Institutional Ethics Panel. Protocols involving more than minimal risk (Categories 2 to 5) must also be submitted to the Ministry of Health for evaluation through EMLAP.
q_1_4_fuente: Standards and Regulation Division – Ministry of Health and Wellness of Jamaica (Chapter: Advisory Panels, paragraph 2); Guidelines for the Conduct of Research on Human Subjects (Chapter: Research Protocol Review, paragraphs 3 and 4).
q_1_5_directa: No. Approval from the local Institutional Ethics Panel is a prerequisite for the study to begin. When submitting the protocol to EMLAP, a copy of the local committee's approval must be included if available at the time of submission.
q_1_5_ampliada: This suggests the local ethical review process may run concurrently with the central regulatory process (submission to the Ministry), although institutional ethical approval remains fundamental. The local institution must review and approve all protocols before they begin.
q_1_5_fuente: Guidelines for the Conduct of Research on Human Subjects (Chapter: Research Protocol Review, paragraphs 3 and 4).
q_1_6_directa: No formal, legally binding accreditation system exists for Research Ethics Committees (RECs) in Jamaica. The country currently relies on operational policies for ethical review. Primary oversight rests centrally with EMLAP at the Ministry of Health and Wellness.
q_1_6_ampliada: Jamaica's regulatory framework for health research is a work in progress, currently lacking a dedicated statutory law establishing a strict accreditation system for RECs. Local institutional committees operate under operational policies and ministerial guidelines that do not carry binding legal weight. These local committees initially evaluate protocols before mandatory national-level review by EMLAP for higher-risk studies. Regional institutions such as CARPHA and CANREC provide technical support and capacity building. However, CANREC does not constitute an official accrediting body for Jamaica, but rather a collaborative network.
q_1_6_fuente: No specific regulation was identified on this point.
q_1_7_directa: No official national public registry of Research Ethics Committees (RECs) directly managed by the Jamaican government is detailed. However, at the regional level, CANREC gathers information on member states' RECs. This effort seeks to promote mutual exchange and harmonization across the Caribbean.
q_1_7_ampliada: Current regulations and guidelines from Jamaica's Ministry of Health and Wellness do not explicitly establish maintaining a public, accessible registry of local RECs. The ethical review system is heavily centralized through EMLAP at the national level. For its part, regional initiatives such as CANREC, supported by CARPHA, seek to integrate information on the various RECs across the Caribbean. However, there is no formal official listing allowing the public to consult recognized or accredited committees operating within its territory.
q_1_7_fuente: No specific regulation was identified on this point.
q_1_8_directa: Yes. Prior authorization is required for importing, selling, or manufacturing a "new drug," and protocols classified in risk Categories 2 to 5 must undergo evaluation by the Ministry of Health.
q_1_8_ampliada: The definition of "new drug" covers any substance or drug combination whose safety and efficacy have not been established in Jamaica. Categories 2 to 5 cover all minimal-risk studies (with or without benefit to the subject) and those with more than minimal risk. Category 1 studies (observation or clinical data collection with no identity protections) may receive an expedited review from the local Medical Officer of Health.
q_1_8_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations, 1975 (LN 65/1975) (Regulation 64, paragraph 1); Guidelines for the Conduct of Research on Human Subjects (Chapter: Research Protocol Categories, paragraphs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5); (Chapter: Research Protocol Review, paragraph 2).
q_2_1_directa: Not specified in official regulations.
q_2_1_ampliada: Neither the Food and Drugs Act nor its Regulations offer an explicit definition of the term "sponsor" in the clinical trial context; instead, they focus on the responsibilities of the new drug's manufacturer or importer. Within the Ethical Guidelines, responsibility for safeguarding subjects' well-being falls on the investigator or principal investigator.
q_2_1_fuente: No specific regulation was identified on this point.
q_2_2_directa: Yes, when the applicant for a new drug license is not the manufacturer itself, appointing a local agent or representative in Jamaica is required.
q_2_2_ampliada: Jamaican regulations, focused on product regulation, establish requirements through the "new drug" licensing process. The Food and Drugs Regulations, 1975 specify that the license application to the Minister must include the name and address of an agent or representative on the island for the manufacturer, in cases where the applicant and the manufacturer are different entities. A foreign sponsor acting as the license applicant for an investigational product manufactured by a third party must therefore appoint a local representative to meet this requirement.
q_2_2_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations, 1975 (LN 65/1975) (Regulation 66).
q_2_3_directa: Yes. To import, sell, or manufacture a new drug, the applicant (implicit sponsor) must obtain a license from the Minister and submit a complete description of the drug, details of purity and safety control tests, draft labels, and safety and approval certificates from the country-of-origin authorities.
q_2_3_ampliada: Requirements for the sponsor (or license applicant) are rigorous and focus on product documentation. It must provide the test history certifying identity and purity, and pay an initial fee of five thousand dollars ($5,000) for the new drug license.
q_2_3_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations, 1975 (LN 65/1975) (Regulation 65, paragraph 1); (Regulation 65, paragraph 2, sub-paragraphs a, c, d, e, f, g, and h).
q_2_4_directa: Not specified in official regulations.
q_2_4_ampliada: The Food and Drugs Act and Regulations govern the manufacturer, importer, and investigator roles, but no provision or guideline is provided defining or establishing specific requirements for a Contract Research Organization (CRO) acting in conducting clinical trials in the country.
q_2_4_fuente: No specific regulation was identified on this point.
q_2_5_directa: Yes, requirements exist for selecting research sites in Jamaica, focused on the facility's ability to guarantee safety. Protocols must detail the proposed sites, paying special attention to the facilities available for participants' comfort. The availability of emergency procedures for unanticipated events must also be documented.
q_2_5_ampliada: The regulatory framework requires a clinical trial's evaluation to include a detailed review of the site where the research will be conducted. Under the Ministry of Health and Wellness's guidelines, sites must be ensured to have adequate facilities and equipment for patients' well-being. The research site must have the capacity to manage adverse events or medical emergencies during the study. In addition, when the proposed site includes a hospital, obtaining express permission from the Senior Medical Officer (SMO) or the Director of that facility before starting is a mandatory requirement. The SRD also oversees these public and private health facilities' compliance with the country's current quality standards.
q_2_5_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations, 1975 (LN 65/1975) (Regulation 71, paragraph 1, sub-paragraphs a and d); Guidelines for the Conduct of Research on Human Subjects (Chapter: Fair Selection of Subjects, paragraph 1).
q_2_6_directa: Yes, specific requirements exist requiring investigators to be fully qualified by education, training, and experience. The Principal Investigator (PI) must demonstrate professional competence to conduct the study. This generally requires being duly registered and current with the Medical Council of Jamaica or another relevant regulatory body.
q_2_6_ampliada: A clinical trial's sponsor has the legal and ethical responsibility to select competent investigators and provide them with the required technical information. National guidelines require the research protocol to include the names, addresses, and specific roles of all investigators, collaborators, and supervisors. Who will carry out procedures on participants must be explicitly detailed, and the prior training they have received must be specified. The Principal Investigator acts as the team leader and is directly responsible for overseeing the administration of investigational products. For studies conducted by students, these must be under the direct supervision of a trained person recognized by the local health authorities, such as the Medical Officer of Health.
q_2_6_fuente: Guidelines for the Conduct of Research on Human Subjects (Chapter: Fair Selection of Subjects, paragraph 1).
q_2_7_directa: Yes. For research involving more than minimal risk, the informed consent process must include an explanation of whether compensation and medical treatment are available in the event of injury.
q_2_7_ampliada: If the risk is more than minimal, the consent document must detail what the compensation and medical treatment consist of, and where more information can be obtained. It is a fundamental ethical requirement that the consent information not contain language appearing to exempt the sponsor, investigator, or institution from liability for negligence.
q_2_7_fuente: Guidelines for the Conduct of Research on Human Subjects (Chapter: Informed Consent, paragraph 8, section "For research involving more than minimal risk"); (Chapter: Confidentiality, paragraph 2).
q_3_1_directa: Yes. The submission must include the detailed study protocol with the hypothesis, scientific rationale, study design, and risk/benefit assessment. For a new drug, detailed product information is required, including ingredients, dosage, claims, safety/purity control tests, and a draft label.
q_3_1_ampliada: Essential documents also include the names of investigators and their responsibilities, the research sites, the number of subjects, the proposed duration, a copy of the informed consent form, and the data collection and analysis procedures. Safety and approval certificates from the authorities in the new drug's manufacturing/exporting country must also be attached.
q_3_1_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations, 1975 (LN 65/1975) (Regulation 65, paragraph 2); Guidelines for the Conduct of Research on Human Subjects (Chapter: Guidelines for Preparing Research Protocols, sections 2, 4, 5, 8, and 11).
q_3_2_directa: Yes. Submitting protocols to EMLAP must be electronic and accompanied by a physical (paper) copy.
q_3_2_ampliada: The regulation specifies that all submissions must be electronic. For long-duration studies, periodic updates must be sent to the Ministry's EMLAP.
q_3_2_fuente: Guidelines for the Conduct of Research on Human Subjects (Chapter: Research Protocol Review, paragraph 5).
q_3_3_directa: Yes. Submitting protocols to EMLAP should allow a lead time of four to six weeks for approval. The Minister will notify whether a new drug license application is satisfactory within one hundred and twenty days of its submission.
q_3_3_ampliada: The four-to-six-week time frame is a necessary estimate for the protocol's ethical and legal evaluation. The 120-day time frame applies to the Minister's decision on the new drug license.
q_3_3_fuente: Guidelines for the Conduct of Research on Human Subjects (Chapter: Research Protocol Review, paragraph 5); Food and Drugs Regulations, 1975 (LN 65/1975) (Regulation 68, sub-paragraph a).
q_3_4_directa: Yes. The license to import, sell, or manufacture a new drug requires payment of an initial fee of five thousand dollars ($5,000) in place of the regular registration fee.
q_3_4_ampliada: In addition to the $5,000 new drug license fee, importing a drug requires a permit with a fee of two hundred dollars ($200) for up to ten products.
q_3_4_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations, 1975 (LN 65/1975) (Regulation 65, paragraph 1, sub-paragraph b); (Regulation 43, paragraph 1); (Regulation 40, paragraph 1, sub-paragraph b).
q_3_5_directa: Not specified in official regulations.
q_3_5_ampliada: Although research protocol files submitted to the Medical Officer of Health are open to public inspection, the current regime does not establish an explicit requirement to register the clinical trial on a public platform (such as ClinicalTrials.gov or a national registry) before the study begins.
q_3_5_fuente: No specific regulation was identified on this point.
q_3_6_directa: Yes. The new drug licensing process requires submitting a certificate from the competent authority in the manufacturing/exporting country certifying that the drug is approved for use in that country, and the conditions under which it may be used or sold.
q_3_6_ampliada: A certificate in English, issued by an official body in the manufacturing country, attesting to the new drug's safety and demonstrating that body has the expertise and facilities to carry out adequate safety testing, is also required. All imported products must also fully conform to the law of the country where they were manufactured.
q_3_6_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations, 1975 (LN 65/1975) (Regulation 65, paragraph 2, sub-paragraph g and h); Food and Drugs Act, 1964 (Act 46 of 1964) (Section 4, paragraph 1).
q_3_7_directa: The process combines the Minister's technical approval for using the new drug and the protocol's ethical review, requiring both authorizations before starting.
q_3_7_ampliada:
Protocol Development: The Principal Investigator (PI) and the Sponsor prepare the Clinical Research Protocol, including the new drug's preclinical/clinical documentation and the informed consent form.

Institutional Ethical Approval: The protocol is submitted to the local Institutional Ethics Panel, which must review and approve it.

New Drug License Application: The Sponsor/Importer applies for the license from the Minister, submitting the product documentation (ingredients, control tests, labels, foreign certificates) and paying the $5,000 fee. This application must be resolved within 120 days.

Investigational Use Authorization: The PI requests and obtains the Minister's written authorization to conduct research with the new drug, confirming their qualifications and adequate facilities.

Submission to the Ministry of Health: The protocol is submitted to EMLAP, including local ethical approval (if available), in electronic format plus a physical copy. An evaluation time of 4 to 6 weeks should be expected.

Authorization to Begin: Once the new drug license (or investigational use permit) and the Ministry of Health's ethical and regulatory approval (MoH Panel) have been received, the trial may begin.
q_3_7_fuente: Guidelines for the Conduct of Research on Human Subjects (Chapter: Research Protocol Review, paragraphs 3 and 5); Food and Drugs Regulations, 1975 (LN 65/1975) (Regulation 65, 68, and 71).
q_4_1_directa: Yes. For new drugs imported for research purposes, the packages' inner and outer labels must bear the statement: "To be used for investigational purposes only."
q_4_1_ampliada: This specific requirement ensures the investigational drug is not distributed or sold for other purposes. In addition, general labeling for any drug must include the proper or common name, the manufacturer's/distributor's name/address, the batch number (if for parenteral use), and adequate instructions for use.
q_4_1_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations, 1975 (LN 65/1975) (Regulation 71, paragraph 1, sub-paragraph c); (Regulation 44, paragraph 1).
q_4_2_directa: Yes, the drug must have been manufactured, prepared, packaged, and tested under "adequate conditions," which implies using good pharmaceutical practices to ensure the product's identity, potency, and purity.
q_4_2_ampliada: "Adequate conditions" include the construction and finish of the facilities to allow for efficient cleaning, prevent contamination, having technically trained supervisory staff, and using quality controls testing each batch of raw material and dosage-form product to guarantee its identity, potency, and purity.
q_4_2_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations, 1975 (LN 65/1975) (Regulation 42, paragraphs 1 and 2, sub-paragraphs a, d, f, and g).
q_4_3_directa: No. A clinical trial's approval for a new drug is conditional on obtaining an import/use/sale license from the Minister or, in the research context, the Minister's written authorization to the investigator for the drug's use.
q_4_3_ampliada: A new drug may not be imported without a license or permit. However, the Minister may specifically authorize importing a set quantity of a new drug for use by qualified investigators, exclusively for the purpose of collecting clinical and scientific data.
q_4_3_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations, 1975 (LN 65/1975) (Regulation 65, paragraph 1); (Regulation 71, paragraph 1, sub-paragraphs a and b).
q_5_1_directa: Yes. Reports of serious, valid Adverse Drug Reactions (ADRs) must be submitted to the National Pharmacovigilance Centre (NPvC) within 15 calendar days of the date of receipt. Anyone receiving a report of unexpected side effects, injury, or toxicity associated with new drug studies must immediately inform the Minister.
q_5_1_ampliada: The SRD is the National Pharmacovigilance Centre and report repository. Marketing Authorisation Holders (MAHs) may use the local PharmWatch Drug Monitoring Reporting Forms or the CIOMS form for reports occurring in Jamaica. Non-serious reports must be submitted within 90 days.
q_5_1_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations, 1975 (LN 65/1975) (Regulation 70); Pharmacovigilance – Ministry of Health and Wellness of Jamaica (Chapter: Post-marketing Surveillance Programme in Jamaica, paragraph 3); (Chapter: Reporting of Suspected Adverse Reactions, paragraphs 6 and 7).
q_5_2_directa: Yes. Marketing Authorisation Holders (MAHs) must share Periodic Benefit-Risk Evaluation Reports (PBRERs) or Periodic Safety Update Reports (PSURs) with the SRD.
q_5_2_ampliada: Submitting these periodic reports follows a specific timeline: every 6 months until marketing, every 6 months for the first two years on the market, annually for the next two years, and every 3 years thereafter. PBRERs covering 6- or 12-month intervals must be submitted within 70 calendar days of the data-lock point.
q_5_2_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations, 1975 (LN 65/1975). Pharmacovigilance – Ministry of Health and Wellness of Jamaica (Chapter: Post-marketing Surveillance Programme in Jamaica, paragraph 10); (Chapter: Post-marketing Surveillance Programme in Jamaica, section "PBRERs must be submitted based on the following timelines").
q_5_3_directa: Yes. When the study extends over a prolonged period, the investigator must submit periodic study updates at six-month intervals, and a summary of findings, to the Chairman of the Ministry of Health's EMLAP.
q_5_3_ampliada: In addition to these semi-annual reports, the principal investigator is required to inform the Medical Officer of Health if any adverse event is observed, or if there are deviations or a desire to alter the approved protocol.
q_5_3_fuente: Guidelines for the Conduct of Research on Human Subjects (Chapter: Research Protocol Review, paragraph 6); (Chapter: Research Oversight, paragraph 1).
q_5_4_directa: Yes. Any desired protocol alteration, and any instance where procedures deviate from what was originally approved, must be reported to the Medical Officer of Health. A material change to a new drug (e.g., in potency, dosage, or label) requires a new license application.
q_5_4_ampliada: Modifying a new drug's conditions of use, dosage, or pharmaceutical form is considered a material change and requires submitting a new license application with all the change's details. Changes affecting the protocol's conduct must also be reported to the local authority for review.
q_5_4_fuente: Food and Drugs Regulations, 1975 (LN 65/1975) (Regulation 66, sub-paragraphs a, b, c, d, and e); Guidelines for the Conduct of Research on Human Subjects (Chapter: Research Oversight, paragraph 1).
q_5_5_directa: Not specified in official regulations.
q_5_5_ampliada: While the regulation is clear on the need to report available compensation for injury during the study, it does not explicitly address whether the sponsor has a regulatory obligation to continue supplying the investigational treatment to subjects once the clinical trial has formally concluded.
q_5_5_fuente: No specific regulation was identified on this point.
q_6_1_directa: Yes. Jamaica's Data Protection Act, 2020 is the main legislation applicable to personal data protection in clinical trials.
q_6_1_ampliada:
The Data Protection Act (DPA), 2020, fully in force since December 2023, establishes the legal framework for processing personal data in Jamaica. It is directly applicable to clinical trials, as it regulates the processing of "sensitive personal data," which explicitly includes data on physical and mental health, genetic data, and biometric data. Under this law, the trial's sponsor and institution act as "Data Controllers" and have the following key obligations:
Complying with 8 Data Protection Standards: Including fair, lawful processing, purpose limitation, data minimization, and security.
Obtaining Explicit Consent: Processing sensitive personal data requires the data subject's (trial participant's) explicit, informed consent, which may be withdrawn at any time.
Guaranteeing Subjects' Rights: Participants have the right to access their data, request its rectification or deletion, and object to processing in certain circumstances.
Notifying Security Breaches: Any security breach affecting personal data must be reported to the Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC) within 72 hours.
Regulating International Transfers: Personal data must not be transferred outside Jamaica unless the receiving country guarantees an adequate level of protection. Oversight of the law rests with the Information Commissioner, and penalties for non-compliance are severe.
q_6_1_fuente: The Data Protection Act, 2020; Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC) Jamaica.
q_6_2_directa: Not specified in official regulations.
q_6_2_ampliada: Vaccines are classified as Schedule 4 Drugs (prescription-only medicines) under the Food and Drugs Regulations, 1975. They are therefore subject to the general "new drug" regulatory requirements (licensing, safety testing, investigational use). No specific guideline or regulation is identified governing the particular aspects of vaccine clinical research.
q_6_2_fuente: No specific regulation was identified on this point.
q_6_3_directa: Not specified in official regulations.
q_6_3_ampliada: The current regulatory framework contains no specific provisions or guidelines detailing the technical or procedural requirements for collecting, storing, handling, or subsequently using human biological samples (such as tissue or blood) obtained specifically within a clinical research framework.
q_6_3_fuente: No specific regulation was identified on this point.
q_6_4_directa: Yes. The Guidelines for Research on Human Subjects require the investigator to indicate and justify the inclusion of vulnerable populations, such as children, the elderly, persons with physical disabilities, or pregnant women.
q_6_4_ampliada: Investigators must be aware of the special issues involved in researching vulnerable populations, also including prisoners or persons with economic or educational disadvantages. The protocol must detail the justification for including or not including specific groups (such as women or ethnic groups), and, where necessary, how gender balance will be ensured.
q_6_4_fuente: Guidelines for the Conduct of Research on Human Subjects (Chapter: Procedures for Good Ethical Practice, paragraph 5, sections 3 and 4); (Chapter: Fair Selection of Subjects, paragraph 2).

q_1_1_directa: The main regulatory authority for clinical trials is not explicitly defined in the documents, but the Direction de la Pharmacie, du Médicament et de la Médecine Traditionnelle (Directorate of Pharmacy, Medicines and Traditional Medicine, DPM/MT) is responsible for regulating pharmaceutical products, the Direction d'Epidémiologie, de Laboratoires, de Recherche (Directorate of Epidemiology, Laboratories, and Research, DELR) is responsible for planning, promoting, and developing research, and the Comité National de Bioéthique (National Bioethics Committee, CNB) is the main body for the ethical approval of research protocols.
q_1_1_ampliada: Although the framework for medicine authorization is managed by the DPM/MT, the fundamental approval for beginning a research project rests with the CNB, and starting without its ruling is considered a serious ethical violation. The DELR, within the Ministère de la Santé Publique et de la Population (Ministry of Public Health and Population, MSPP), is responsible for planning, promoting, and developing research.
q_1_1_fuente: Décret du 28 décembre 2005 portant Organisation du Ministère de la Santé Publique et de la Population (MSPP) (Article 35, Article 36), Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique Pour approbation De protocole de recherche (Décembre 2014) (page 1).
q_1_2_directa: The fundamental strategic regulation is the Politique Nationale de Recherche en Santé (PNRS), published in January 2020.
q_1_2_ampliada: This document defines the institutional framework and broad strategies for developing evidence-based research in Haiti. It is complemented by the 2005 Décret organizing the MSPP and creating the DELR, as well as by the 2014 Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique governing operational ethical approval.
q_1_2_fuente: Politique Nationale de Recherche en Santé (Janvier 2020); Décret du 28 décembre 2005 portant Organisation du MSPP; Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique Pour approbation De protocole de recherche (Décembre 2014).
q_1_3_directa: No specific regulation exists in public documentation governing Clinical Trial Authorization by the medicines regulatory authority (DPM/MT). Research regulation centers on ethical approval through the CNB.
q_1_3_ampliada: Haiti's regulatory framework for research involving human subjects operates under an "ethical gateway" model. The main, most detailed regulation is the Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique. This document unequivocally establishes that starting research without the CNB's prior approval constitutes a "serious ethical violation." This positions the CNB as the primary and, in practice, only body granting authorization to begin research activities. The DPM/MT's role, per available regulations such as the Loi 1955 and the Marketing Authorization (AMM) procedures, focuses on the pharmaceutical product itself: its quality, registration, import, and post-marketing pharmacovigilance.
q_1_3_fuente: Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique Pour approbation De protocole de recherche (Décembre 2014), Standards for Sanitary Registration and Laboratory Accreditation (DPM/MT) / Enregistrement d'un laboratoire et obtention d'AMM.
q_1_4_directa: Yes, approval from the CNB is required for research protocols.
q_1_4_ampliada: Submitting 12 complete copies of the protocol in French to the CNB to obtain its ruling is mandatory. The committee expressly warns that starting a research project without the CNB's ruling is considered a serious ethical violation.
q_1_4_fuente: Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique Pour approbation De protocole de recherche (Décembre 2014) (page 1, section 3).
q_1_5_directa: Yes, approval from an ethics committee at the investigator's organization (institutional or the sponsor's) is an indispensable prerequisite for submitting the protocol for the CNB's review. The sequence with respect to the DPM/MT is undefined, as no formal process exists for requesting clinical trial authorization from that entity.
q_1_5_ampliada: Haiti's ethical approval process is hierarchical and sequential, not parallel. The Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique explicitly require the submission dossier to include "a copy of your organization's ethics committee approval." This means a sponsor must first obtain approval from its own ethics committee (or a local institutional committee, if applicable) before beginning the process with the national ethics authority (CNB). This requirement establishes a clear sequence of steps: 1) Institutional/sponsor ethical approval; 2) Submission to the CNB with the prior approval attached. Since no formal clinical trial authorization process exists before the DPM/MT, the question of its sequencing is moot. In practice, any DPM/MT procedure related to the investigational product (e.g., an import permit) would be handled separately from, or after, obtaining the CNB's approval, which is what enables the study to begin.
q_1_5_fuente: Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique Pour approbation De protocole de recherche (Décembre 2014) (page 2).
q_1_6_directa: No formal national accreditation system for Research Ethics Committees (RECs) exists. Ethical review of research involving human subjects is primarily centralized at the CNB, which acts as the national body for protocol ethical evaluation.
q_1_6_ampliada: The Republic of Haiti's institutional framework does not provide for a legal or administrative mechanism to formally accredit, register, or oversee multiple Research Ethics Committees nationally. A 1999 ministerial decision established the CNB as the body responsible for protecting persons participating in biomedical research. The 2014 Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique subsequently consolidated the CNB's role as the national body responsible for the ethical review of research protocols involving human subjects. In this context, Haiti operates under a functionally centralized ethical evaluation model, in which the CNB is the main reviewing authority, with no national accreditation system applicable to any institutional committees that may exist.
q_1_6_fuente: Décision ministérielle de creation d'un Comité Provisoire de Bio-éthique et de Protection des Personnes (September 1, 1999).
q_1_7_directa: No national public registry of Research Ethics Committees (RECs) exists. Ethical review of biomedical research protocols is channeled mainly through the CNB, with no national registration or publication system of accredited committees in operation.
q_1_7_ampliada: Haitian regulations and institutions do not provide for creating or maintaining an administrative public registry to identify or validate Research Ethics Committees. Under the 2014 Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique, research protocols involving human subjects must be submitted to the CNB for ethical evaluation, establishing a functionally centralized national ethical review model. In the absence of a formal accreditation system or structured oversight of institutional committees, no public or government database listing authorized RECs has been developed. Consequently, validating a study's applicable ethical review is done through the CNB's issued approval and the corresponding documentation included in the protocol's file, rather than by consulting a national public registry.
q_1_7_fuente: Décision ministérielle de création d'un Comité Provisoire de Bio-éthique et de Protection des Personnes (1999).
q_1_8_directa: Yes. Any research project whose protocol must be approved by the CNB must receive its prior ruling, as starting a research project without the CNB's ruling is considered a serious ethical violation.
q_1_8_ampliada: The sources regulate research in general through the CNB's procedures. In addition, the DPM/MT's role is to control the quality of imported medicines, whether generic or branded, through the registration system.
q_1_8_fuente: Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique Pour approbation De protocole de recherche (Décembre 2014) (page 1, section 3), Décret du 28 décembre 2005 portant Organisation du Ministère de la Santé Publique et de la Population (MSPP) (Article 35).
q_2_1_directa: Not specified in official regulations.
q_2_1_ampliada: Existing regulations focus on defining the responsibilities of those requesting laboratory accreditation and sanitary registration (AMM), referring to a "local manufacturer or a representative of pharmaceutical products." The CNB's documentation focuses on the principal investigator's obligations. No formal definition of a clinical trial "sponsor" is provided.
q_2_1_fuente: Standards for Sanitary Registration and Laboratory Accreditation (DPM/MT) / Enregistrement d'un laboratoire et obtention d'AMM (pages 1, 2), Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique Pour approbation De protocole de recherche (Décembre 2014) (page 1).
q_2_2_directa: The regulation does not specify an explicit obligation for a foreign clinical trial sponsor to have a legal representative domiciled in Haiti. However, this is a de facto requirement due to pharmaceutical product import and distribution regulations.
q_2_2_ampliada: Although research regulations do not define the "sponsor's legal representative" role, regulations governing pharmaceutical products functionally make it indispensable. The process for obtaining a Marketing Authorization (AMM) is initiated by a "local manufacturer or a representative of pharmaceutical products." More importantly, import regulations require an "importer" to request the corresponding permits from the Ministry of Commerce and the Ministry of Health. The 2023 Normes de Fabrication, d'Importation et de Distribution des Médicaments detail the licensing requirements for local pharmaceutical establishments (agencies, depots), which must be under the responsibility of a licensed Haitian pharmacist. A foreign sponsor cannot import the investigational product itself; it must hire an authorized local entity (an importing agency) to act as its representative for all import and customs procedures before the DPM/MT. This entity becomes, in practice, the sponsor's representative for product-related matters.
q_2_2_fuente: Standards for Sanitary Registration and Laboratory Accreditation (DPM/MT) / Enregistrement d'un laboratoire et obtention d'AMM, Normes de Fabrication, d'Importation et de Distribution des Médicaments (Octobre 2023), Haiti - Import Requirements & Documentation.
q_2_3_directa: Not specified in official regulations.
q_2_3_ampliada: Detailed regulatory requirements are directed at laboratories seeking accreditation (company profile, GMP certificate, manufacturing license), which apply to the investigational product's manufacturer. However, no requirements are established for a "clinical trial sponsor" as a role distinct from the entity responsible for the product.
q_2_3_fuente: No specific regulation was identified on this point.
q_2_4_directa: Not specified in official regulations.
q_2_4_ampliada: Current regulations make no mention of Contract Research Organizations (CROs) or the requirements these entities must meet to act on a sponsor's behalf.
q_2_4_fuente: No specific regulation was identified on this point.
q_2_5_directa: Yes. Requirements exist in Haiti for selecting research sites, evaluated within the CNB's ethical approval process. Sites must demonstrate sufficient infrastructure, human resources, and operational capacity to guarantee participant safety and the clinical study's proper management.
q_2_5_ampliada: Under the December 2014 Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique, a protocol's ethical evaluation in Haiti includes verifying the fitness of the site where the research will be conducted. As part of the file submitted to the CNB, the sponsor or investigator must provide information demonstrating the site has adequate conditions for safely conducting the study. This evaluation covers, among other aspects, the existence of spaces ensuring participants' confidentiality and privacy, availability of appropriate clinical equipment, data management and safeguarding systems, and storage and preservation capacity for investigational products (including cold chain, where applicable). The CNB and/or the MSPP may also require additional information or conduct checks aimed at confirming the establishment's capacity to respond to adverse events and meet international biosafety and Good Clinical Practice standards. These requirements apply within a functionally centralized ethical review model, with no independent national system for licensing or accrediting research sites.
q_2_5_fuente: Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique Pour approbation De protocole de recherche (Décembre 2014). Ministère de la Santé Publique et de la Population (MSPP).
q_2_6_directa: Yes. The Principal Investigator must demonstrate adequate professional qualifications, a license to practice medicine, and sufficient experience to conduct the proposed study.
q_2_6_ampliada: The 2014 Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique establish that every protocol submitted for ethical evaluation must include detailed information on the Principal Investigator and the research team. As part of this review, the CNB requires submitting the investigator's up-to-date curriculum vitae, documentation certifying their professional training, and evidence of their ability to carry out the study in accordance with accepted ethical and scientific principles. In practice, the Principal Investigator must have relevant medical or health training and authorization to practice professionally in Haiti under the MSPP's supervision. Sponsors and Contract Research Organizations also typically require Good Clinical Practice (GCP) training, in line with international standards applicable to research involving human subjects. These requirements are evaluated within the national ethical review process conducted by the CNB, which acts as the central body for the ethical evaluation of biomedical research protocols in the country.
q_2_6_fuente: Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique Pour approbation De protocole de recherche (Décembre 2014). Ministère de la Santé Publique et de la Population (MSPP).
q_2_7_directa: Yes. The consent form must specify, where applicable, the compensation to be given to participants, and must detail what is planned in the event of harm.
q_2_7_ampliada: The description of what is planned in the event of harm must include payment for time spent, travel or inconvenience, the treatment available, and its cost. The CNB Chairman's name and contact details must also be specified as the contact point for ethical issues.
q_2_7_fuente: Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique Pour approbation De protocole de recherche (Décembre 2014) (page 3).
q_3_1_directa: Yes. The submission (to the CNB) requires a dossier of 12 copies including: the cover letter signed by the principal investigator (guaranteeing adherence to the protocol and Good Practice), a copy of their ethics certificate, the complete protocol in French (paginated), and the consent form in French and Creole.
q_3_1_ampliada: The protocol must detail the rationale, objectives, methodology, timeline, budget, laboratory standards, and techniques. Including the investigators' CVs, the approval from the investigator's own organization's ethics committee, and stating the publication rules and reporting deadlines are also mandatory.
q_3_1_fuente: Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique Pour approbation De protocole de recherche (Décembre 2014) (page 1, page 2).
q_3_2_directa: Yes. Submission to the CNB is physical, through submitting 12 complete packages (envelopes).
q_3_2_ampliada: The CNB notes that only one envelope should be addressed to the Chairman, and that "colis postaux" (postal parcels) are not collected at Haiti's Post Office. Correspondence with the committee must be written in French or Creole, Haiti's official languages.
q_3_2_fuente: Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique Pour approbation De protocole de recherche (Décembre 2014) (page 1, page 5).
q_3_3_directa: Yes. The CNB's review of the dossier can take up to 3 months, so the dossier must be submitted well in advance.
q_3_3_ampliada: For a dossier to be reviewed at the monthly meeting (the second Monday of each month), it must be received by the committee at least fifteen (15) business days in advance.
q_3_3_fuente: Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique Pour approbation De protocole de recherche (Décembre 2014) (page 1, page 3).
q_3_4_directa: Not specified in official regulations.
q_3_4_ampliada: While DPM/MT regulations set fees for medicines' sanitary registration (AMM) (5,000 gourdes for branded products and 2,500 gourdes for generics), CNB documentation does not mention whether fees are charged for reviewing research protocols.
q_3_4_fuente: No specific regulation was identified on this point.
q_3_5_directa: Not specified in official regulations.
q_3_5_ampliada: The regulations reviewed do not establish an obligation to publicly register a clinical trial in a database before it begins.
q_3_5_fuente: No specific regulation was identified on this point.
q_3_6_directa: Yes, though only for recognition mechanisms for supporting technical documents, such as Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) certification, which may be issued by a competent body (WHO, ISO, or others), provided it is legalized and validated.
q_3_6_ampliada: While internationally issued GMP documentation is accepted, no recognition process is specified for foreign RECs' complete ethical approvals; in fact, the CNB requires a copy of the investigator's own organization's ethics committee approval as part of the file, implying a mandatory local review requirement by the CNB.
q_3_6_fuente: Standards for Sanitary Registration and Laboratory Accreditation (DPM/MT) / Enregistrement d'un laboratoire et obtention d'AMM (page 2), Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique Pour approbation De protocole de recherche (Décembre 2014) (page 2).
q_3_7_directa: The process begins with obtaining the investigator's own institutional ethical approval and confirming the principal investigator's qualifications, followed by preparing 12 dossier copies and physically submitting them to the CNB.
q_3_7_ampliada:
1) The Principal Investigator (PI) obtains ethical approval from their organization and their ethics course certificate.

2) A competent Haitian counterpart is established on the team.

3) The sponsor/PI prepares 12 copies of the protocol and supporting documentation (in French/Creole).

4) The dossier is physically sent to the CNB's address.

5) The CNB receives the complete file at least 15 business days before its meeting.

6) The CNB issues its ruling, which is mandatory before research may begin. (Note: If the pharmaceutical product is not on the national list, the manufacturer/representative must apply for laboratory accreditation and sanitary registration (AMM) from the DPM/MT.)
q_3_7_fuente: Procédures du Comité National de Bioéthique Pour approbation De protocole de recherche (Décembre 2014) (page 1, page 2, page 3), Standards for Sanitary Registration and Laboratory Accreditation (DPM/MT) / Enregistrement d'un laboratoire et obtention d'AMM (page 1).
q_4_1_directa: Not specified in official regulations.
q_4_1_ampliada: While the 1955 Law requires every dispensed medicine to carry a label with pharmacy information, instructions for use, and identification, no specific labeling requirements exist in the sources for Investigational Products (IPs) used in clinical trials.
q_4_1_fuente: No specific regulation was identified on this point.
q_4_2_directa: Yes, a recently dated Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) Certificate, issued by a competent body (WHO, ISO, or others), legalized and validated, is required.
q_4_2_ampliada: This requirement applies to the sanitary registration process, and may be replaced by an inspection of the manufacturing laboratories by a DPM/MT team, at the applicant's expense. An ISO Certificate is also required for laboratories manufacturing injectable products.
q_4_2_fuente: Standards for Sanitary Registration and Laboratory Accreditation (DPM/MT) / Enregistrement d'un laboratoire et obtention d'AMM (pages 1, 2, 3).
q_4_3_directa: Not specified in official regulations.
q_4_3_ampliada: The Autorisation de Dédouanement (Customs Clearance Authorization, AD) is only requested for products that already have a DPM/MT-issued Marketing Authorization (AMM). Since IPs generally do not hold an AMM, the process for importing a product intended exclusively for research and approved only by the CNB is not documented in the sources.
q_4_3_fuente: Standards for Sanitary Registration and Laboratory Accreditation (DPM/MT) / Enregistrement d'un laboratoire et obtention d'AMM (page 1).
